sections.workload:
The workload includes regular attendance checks, four written assignments with optional coding, and one larger programming assignment in a Kaggle style. In addition, there is a mid-term and a final exam, both open-book with limited cheatsheets. However, the assignments and kaggle competition are not difficult.

The assignments account for 60% of the grade, so you do not need to worry about the grade of the examination since the grading is very lenient, and both the midterm and final exams only account for 20% each.

sections.content: The course content primarily covers the fundamental principles of machine learning, with a significant portion dedicated to statistics and linear algebra. Additionally, it explores the underlying principles of Transformers.
sections.teaching: Junxian is a highly knowledgeable instructor who clearly possesses a deep understanding of the subject matter. His insights on VAE are particularly insightful (though I must admit the course is a bit challenging for me).
sections.grading: This course is graded fairly leniently. I did my best to complete all the assignments, which were somewhat challenging for me and took a lot of time. If you have a solid grasp of the prerequisite math concepts, it shouldn't take too long. My midterm and final exam scores were average, but after the comprehensive assignments and project, I ended up with a B+.
sections.workload: This isn't an easy course. In fact, it consumed a significant amount of my time—averaging an entire day each week just to complete the assignments—while constantly worrying about failing. This is particularly painful for a PG student who must devote most of their energy to balancing research and coursework.

sections.content: The material covers fundamental Python topics such as if/else statements, for loops, lists, dictionaries, basic classes, functions/methods, and recursion. It also includes Turtle graphics, a library that lets you create drawings by controlling “turtles” (which act like brushes or pens) through code. The content should be very straightforward for anyone with prior programming experience. However, be cautious with Python’s data types since the language is type-optional, and type hints won’t be taught or tested in exams.
sections.teaching: Alex Lam, the professor, teaches well and often repeats key points to ensure clarity, recognizing that programming concepts can initially be confusing and need reinforcement. That said, I personally found the lectures unnecessary since I already had programming experience and skipped most of them, so I can’t comment much on the teaching overall.
sections.grading:
There are two grading schemes:

24% midterm + 36% labs + 40% final
OR 42% labs + 58% final
The course includes 7 labs plus an introductory lab. Three labs are graded out of 100. The labs themselves are relatively easy, but you must be meticulous because there are usually no partial marks—one small error causing your program to fail a test case can cost you up to 20% of that lab’s score (this actually happened to me). Lab averages typically range from 90 to 100 with a standard deviation of 8 to 10.

The midterm is fairly simple if you’re careful and review your answers. Since the exam is remote, you should have enough time, especially if you have prior programming experience. The midterm average was about 71.9 with a standard deviation around 21.4.

In contrast, the final exam is very challenging. Time is tight, leaving little room to double-check answers. The questions are tricky and sometimes misleading—for example, multiplying a number by 2 when the number is actually a string, not an integer. Extreme caution is required. This semester’s final average was 48.57 with a standard deviation of 19.29.

One strategy is to treat the final as a typing test by quickly typing out the code they don’t allow you to copy. If you can type fast (90-100 words per minute), this approach can reduce stress and improve performance.
sections.workload: The workload is very light. There are 7 labs plus an introductory lab; only 3 labs are submitted and graded. The non-graded labs are optional but worth reviewing since their content often appears on the final exam. The labs are easy as long as you can follow instructions and apply basic programming skills.

sections.content: The contents are comprehensive, covering (1) standard machine learning topics like linear regression, logistic regression, and simple generative models (Naive Bayes), Bias-variance trade-off;  (2) Deep learning models like FFN, CNN, RNN, and Transformer; (3) Deep generative models like VAE, GAN, diffusion models; (4) Reinforcement learning. Each parts are accompanied by hands-on or written assignments to deepen your understanding. So, after studying this course, you should have a good command of basic ideas of machine learning and deep learning. The course is taught using a probabilistic perspective, so a good understanding of probability theory would be beneficial.
sections.teaching: The teaching is good and the explanation is intuitive. The teaching materials and plan are well-designed. The instructor has posted recorded videos that you could watch after class. Also, he is available and responsive on Piazza to answer questions by himself.
sections.grading: Though the final exam is open-book and you may bring up to four cheat sheets, I found the questions not trivial; you need to have a good understanding of the materials covered in the class in order to answer the questions and get high grades. The final exam consists of 64% of the final grade, which I think is a little bit large.
sections.workload: The workload is substantial, comprising 4 written assignments and approximately 5 hands-on assignments to complete. A similarity score exceeding 40% will give you a penalty on the grade, so you need to be careful to answer the questions in the assignment.

sections.content: Covers almost all machine learning models, bert transformer diffusion cnn rnn lstm,rl etc. and reasons in detail about all the formula bases and model bases, you need to follow him carefully in the lead up to each session or you'll get more and more confused.

sections.content: It covers almost all machine learning models, such as bert, transformer diffusion, cnn, rnn, lstm, etc., and reasoning all the formula foundations and model foundations in detail. You need to follow him carefully in the early stage of each class; otherwise, you will understand more and more. (Utilitarianism speaking,) There is no need to attend this course in class. The ppt covers a very wide range of derivations, and the teacher will complete the derivations in great detail. However, most of the questions in the exam are very fragmented explanation questions. You need to ensure that you can basically cover all the knowledge content. Derivations are a "super bonus point" for the exam.
sections.teaching: A very, very, very, very, very, very, very responsible teacher. The lesson preparation is completely serious, and the homework is strictly formulated according to the teaching schedule. Listening to his classes is a kind of enjoyment
sections.grading: The scoring for regular homework is not very lenient. About 10 assignments are given a regular score of around 40
sections.workload: The workload is heavy, with 4 WA and more than 5 HA. The HA assignments are not difficult, but some of the WA questions can be quite challenging. Since it's an electronic assignment, and considering the time spent on typing formulas, some of the proof questions in WA can be postponed for about two hours. I think it's highly likely that I won't be able to solve them during the exam. Sure, part of the reason is that my foundation in mathematics and science is not good enough. Surprisingly, the connection between the exam and the regular homework is very small. The types of questions in the regular homework account for less than 10% of the exam and are almost never included. Even if they are included, the content is extracted from a single homework question and condensed into a 2-point short question, There are approximately three sub-questions. 2+2+5=9 points is included in the homework.

sections.content:
The content covers most of the tranditional machine learning models and goes deep into them, providing you with a comprehensive understanding of the details behind. This courses is more difficult than previous machine learning courses but you can definitely learn a lot from it.
Basically it covers Linear Regression, Logistic regression, Exponential Family, Generalized linear models, Kernel Methods,Kernel methods, SVM,Generative Models,Naive Bayes, MLE, MAP,Generalization, bias-variance tradeoff,Clustering, EM,PCA before midterm.

And Probabilistic Graphical Models,HMM,Neural Networks, backpropagation,Transformer, Variational autoencoder,GANs, Reinforcement Learning, Language models after midterm.

This courses covers much topics while each topic may worth several hours to teach. So it will be a bit rush, but professor tried to deliver all the key points to you in limited time.
sections.teaching: Professor He's teaching is really good. He can explain all the content clearly and in details. The most important thing is that he will tell you his own understanding about the stuff.  However, the content is too much, if you want to make everything clear, you may still need to take some effort after class.
sections.grading:
The professor said the grading will be generous.

And homework has some bonus questions for us to improve the grade. If you master the content in class, you can answer the bonus questions.
sections.workload:
In total there are 4 written homework + 1 coding assignment + midterm exam + final exam.
The 4 written homework helps us review the content in class and extend a bit to learn the topic deeper. It takes some time to do them but it worth spend time.

The professor said the exam will be much easier than homework.

sections.content: Enough, covers most of the necessary techniques. And these are quite inspiring and helped me with my academic research.
sections.teaching: The new professor, so not as good as an experienced one. But overall, he is trying his best to give us a good lesson, I really understand it is not easy for a new professor.
sections.grading: Good, very fair. And I like this course and the instructor style.
sections.workload: a little time-consuming. A lot of maths about the ground theory, we can understand that machine learning itself is not a black box. the problem is only from deep learning.

sections.content: The course is well-organized. The topics were presented in a logical order. The course covers a wide range of useful topics.
sections.teaching: The professor is an excellent teacher who does a great job of explaining complex. The classroom atmosphere is very positive, and the professor is approachable and eager to solve the confusion of students.
sections.grading: If you complete all the assignments and projects seriously, you can certainly earn a good grade in this course. These tasks are very effective in helping you develop important skills and concepts. The exam is also manageable if you review the main knowledge carefully.
sections.workload: There are several assignments in this course that require you to do mathematics derive or coding. While these assignments can take some time to complete, they are worth the effort. They are very effective in helping you develop important skills and concepts, and completing them has helped me better understand the course material.

sections.content:
Introduction to Machine Learning
Math basics: Linear algebra, Calculus, Probability
Linear models: Linear Regression, Logistic Regression and SVM
Convex Optimization: Smoothness, Lasso Regression, Gradient descent, stochastic gradient descent and its variants
Kernel methods
Tree-based method
Deep Learning:
Convolutional Neural Networks
Recurrent Neural Networks
Transformer and NLP
His research field in Machine Learning
AutoML
Trustworthy Machine Learning
sections.teaching: The content of the course has little to do with the assignment, written assignments are related to convex optimization.
sections.grading: Grading is good.
sections.workload:
3(written)+2(programming) assignment
written assignment: derivation, convex, smoothness, hessian matrix, Newton method, lasso regression
programming assignment: CNN, LSTM

sections.content: his course encompasses a wide range of machine learning topics, providing you with a comprehensive understanding of the underlying theory. By completing this course, you will acquire a solid foundation in machine learning.
sections.teaching: Due to the extensive coverage of topics in this course, the teaching pace may be relatively fast.
sections.grading: The examination for this course is conducted with closed books, meaning you won't have access to external references. However, the exam itself is not overly challenging. By diligently following the guidance of the instructor and thoroughly reviewing the lecture notes, you can expect to achieve a high grade.
sections.workload: The workload is a little bit heavy. It requires 4 written assignments first. I choose not to present so I have to finish 6 hands-on assignments as well.

sections.content: The contents are quite comprehensive and the instructor covered almost every aspect in Machine Learning.
sections.teaching: I think the teaching part can be further improved. Dr. Cheng definitely knows what he's talking about but sometimes it's hard to interpret to students. Maybe he can talk louder next time.
sections.grading: You can definitely get high grade as long as you go through the slides thoroughly and listen to the recordings. The first two assignments are quite challenging since they are all mathematical problems. But the following ones become easier with programming problems.
sections.workload: The workload was fine. There are 5 assignments with mathematical problems and programming problems. Each may take around 2-3 days. There are no midterm. And you need to conduct a machine learning-related project and do the presentation. And there is a final.

sections.content: This course includes valuable information on machine learning topics such as probability, regression, RNN, CNN, Transformer, GAN, VAE, and RL. It is highly beneficial and applicable.
sections.teaching:
Nevin is an excellent teacher, and his courses are straightforward to understand. However, he did mention in the first class that his course is not suitable for students without prior knowledge of machine learning. Nonetheless, I believe it could be beneficial for beginners who are willing to put in the effort to learn.
And I think his website about the course is quite clear for students with a lot of useful information about course info, announcements, course materials and RVC videos.
sections.grading:
4 Written Assignments: (4x5%)
Projects: (30%)
Final examination: (50%)
I received a score of 5/5 on most of my homework assignments.
My performance on the final exam was close to the average score but a little higher.
That's A-
sections.workload: I find the workload a bit burdensome. The homework and coding labs require a significant amount of my time almost every week. However, Nevin presented an alternative - an opportunity to work on a machine learning project. Those who choose to take on the team project(2 to 3 students as a team) can avoid completing the ongoing coding labs.

sections.content: This course covers a wide range of topics in Machine Learning. It also introduces new research in the relevant areas. The main focus of the course is the theoretical foundation behind all the ML techniques, which means you need to understand the equations and algorithms thoroughly.
sections.teaching: Prof. ZHANG's course materials are well-prepared. Basically all the questions in the final exam are covered in the course material. He also provides the recordings of the lecture which are useful for revision.
sections.grading: Since this is a PG course the average grading is relatively higher. Around 50% of all students can get A range. The evaluate criteria includes written assignments, programming project/assignments, and a final exam. Students can choose from complete a group project or finish multiple programming assignments. The written assignments are not very hard and the contents are covered in the course material.
sections.workload: The workload is reasonable. All the homework are not very time-consuming. If you have experience in writing research papers, the programming assignment should not be very challenging since there are many existing code online that can be reused and modified.

sections.content: The course contents are nicely designed, covering both theoretical foundations and high-level ideas. The focus of the course is on deep learning techniques such as CNN, RNN, Transformer, VAE, and GAN, as opposed to traditional machine learning algorithms. Brief introductions to algorithms in recent papers are also provided for each topic. It is recommended that students have some basic knowledge of machine learning before taking this course as many topics are covered. The course provides helpful tutorials that teach about programming and hands-on homework. Programming homework gives students the skeleton code, so students know where to start.
sections.teaching: Prof. Zhang is an excellent teacher who provides wonderful intuitions in this course. He delivers the core concepts in more detail and uses a tablet to write notes, which is helpful for students to follow. The course also utilizes Piazza to facilitate question-asking. In addition, the TAs also provide great support to the students. Overall, the course is well-organized and provides a great learning experience.
sections.grading: The final grade for the course is determined by the final exam, which accounts for 50% of the total score, homework, which accounts for 20%, and the project, which accounts for 30%. For the project, students have the option to complete multiple programming assignments or work on a team project related to their chosen topic. The final exam is a reflection of the amount of effort put into the course.
sections.workload: Completing the homework and project assignments for this course can cost quite some time, but the good thing is that you can learn from the well-designed materials. The most time-consuming aspect of the course is reviewing the class materials because of the packed course contents.

sections.content: Course are useful, well prepared, and could be considered as complete deep introductory materials to provide mathematical and implementation know-how of fundamental progression in machine learning.
sections.teaching: Prof. Zhang explained the materials very well. His knowledge is so deep and he went as far as giving an accurate analogy to illustrate his point, and make sure that his points are delivered well to the students.
sections.grading: The grading is generous. 50% will get an A range, and 90% will get a minimum B, I think, but the Prof notes that we are working hard also for other things, so he tries not to make us worried too much about the final exam.
sections.workload: HWs and HAs can be too much for people without basic math and Python, but I reckon the workload is still doable even for people with such conditions. I didn't take the project path, so I can't comment on that.

sections.content: At a high level, this course can be splitted into two modules: fundamentals and recent researches. The fundamentals cover some mathematic basics (e.g., derivatives, matrix calculation, probability theory) and why machine learning works from theory level. This part is derived from UCLA CS 260. The other part focuses on recent advances in deep learning (e.g., transformers, GANs, semi-supervised learning).
sections.teaching: Unsatisfactory. It can be observed that the instructor tries to make things clear. However, most of the time he would waste on the simple concepts and nearly skipped on what's unfamiliar to me (e.g., graph theory). Even some times the instructor receive no response for the question "If someone understands, please raise your hand", leaving an awkward classroom atmosphere.
sections.grading: I think it is like a binary grading. The final is not difficult. For assignments, as long as you can "complete" them, there will be full marks (since the expected outcome for programming and proofs is obvious), otherwise the marks would be low.
sections.workload: The workload can also be splitted into two categories. For programming projects, you may Google it or search Github for the original answers (as I've said in the content section, it basically copies UCLA CS260). It contains just some simple prediction algorithms. However, for the written homework, it would cost a lot of efforts to dig into it since it is proofs to some of mathematical concepts with few reference you can refer to.

sections.content: The topics in the syllabus were quite interesting. Few topics covered are Theory of generalisation, SVM, DNN, etc.
sections.teaching: He partially copied his slides from the course by Prof. Yaser (Caltech), but was not very good at explaining them. I also found it hard to understand what he is speaking as he speaks in a very low voice.
sections.grading:
No consideration was given to whether the student understands the topic, but only whether the answer is ditto copy of what the instructor wishes to see there. Using any other valid definition than what was presented will lead to deduction in marks.  

No explanation is usually given on many assignments like why they deduct marks until you ask explicitly, and even then your request could be ignored indefinitely.

I also found that he himself doesn't understand many concepts, and is extremely hostile toward any sort of discussion about grading.
This was the first course of his career, and I hope he will becomes a better teacher in the future.
sections.workload: Not much workload. Few assignments, one project, and one exam. The instructor never told or have any useful feedback on the project proposal, but was very quick to criticize the final report. I would have preferred if he has given some feedback earlier so we can improve.

sections.content:
The topic includes basic machine learning concepts, linear regression, generalization, RL concepts, generative models, unsupervised learning, etc.

The lecture discusses mostly about theory and the intuition of the machine learning concepts. It is okay to not fully memorize the technical details as long as you understand the intuition.
sections.teaching: Prof Nevin explains the concepts well although sometimes I find it lacking and not clear (maybe due to accent issues).
sections.grading: I thin the grading is okay. Most students can get an A based from the other students I asked.
sections.workload:
If you have experience with coding, then the workload can be good. The other questions in the homework about ML concepts can be easily answered.

In order to have good result in the exam, it is important to undestand the intution of the concepts.

sections.content:
Well Organized, up-to-date content. Nevin updated the content every year actually.

Little programming thing is involved in the lecture; most of the things are about the theory side (but useful).
sections.teaching: Clear enough; easy to follow with a lot of handwriting maths.
sections.grading: Fair enough for most students. Not difficult to get an A for a PG student.
sections.workload:
Okay for me. But some students complain the workload is too high with the writing assignments, program assignments, the project, and the final exam.

The questions in the final exam are similar to those in the writing assignment.

sections.content: The course covers basic concepts of machine learning. The contents are easy to follow and useful.
sections.teaching: The professor and TA are good at teaching and their delivery is really nice.
sections.grading: The professor is very generous. It's easy to get B+ as long as you follow the workload and your exam score is not too low.
sections.workload: The workload is not too light, but not too heavy. Assignments and final exam are not too hard while the project is quite time consuming and hard to get a great score.

sections.content: The content is very useful I think. It is fundamental for all PG students, not only people who work in the machine learning area.
sections.teaching: Nevin Zhang teaches very clearly on both the overall picture and the details. I like him very much.
sections.grading: Good grade, easy to get A or above even for me. I think if you want to promote your GPA, then you should absolutely choose this course.
sections.workload: Very little workload. It is easy to finish the homework and projects. If you do not want to cost too much time, please choose this.

sections.content: Covered many basic aspects of ML, from basic calculations such as backwardpropagation and gradient descent to specific structures such as CNN, LSTM, GAN.
sections.teaching: Nevin is really a good lecturer. He prepared slides carefully, maintained a good pace in class, and answered questions in time.
sections.grading: Grading seems good as far as I am concerned.
sections.workload: Not too much. Written assignments are basic, if you follow the lectures. You need to work on a group project, but you can choose virtually any topic related to ML. Final exam is not so hard, either.

sections.content: I took this course in UG. I would say that this course is the same as what I took. This course will help the student to understand the basic concepts of  machine learning and deep learning. It is very fun to take this course.
sections.teaching:
The professor Nevin L Zhang is nice and give his point accurately;
However, the handwriting is hard to recognize.
sections.grading:
The grading includes 4 assignments and the mid/final exam.
This course only touches on the basics of neural networks-based computer vision. 90% of student can get B+.
sections.workload: Workload is not very high. Totally can handle it. No mid-term, only project and final exam.
